--- title: "Reweighting Floats by Where They Could Have Gone" jupyter: python3 fig-dpi: 300 execute: cache: false --- ## The problem in one sentence Floats drift into some places (often warm, convergent water) more than others, so a plain average of their profiles over-counts those places and runs warm. ## The fix in one sentence Weight each profile by **the area it stands in for**. That area is one over how many floats were *expected* to land at its spot, given where every float actually was a few weeks earlier. **The recipe.** For each float: 1. Take its real position a few cycles ago (its **anchor**). 2. Drift a cloud of particles from the anchor through the model currents plus some random noise. The cloud is everywhere the float could plausibly be now. 3. Spread the float's "one expected profile" evenly over its cloud. A cloud covering 10% of the box has density $1/0.10 = 10$. 4. Stack all floats' clouds. At each real profile, add up the densities of every cloud it falls in. 5. **Weight = 1 / stacked density.** ## Example 1: three floats The clouds here are flat rectangles so the arithmetic is easy. * **A** sits in a jet. The jet keeps it on a narrow track, so its cloud is a thin ribbon covering 1% of the box. Density is $1/0.01 = 100$, so its weight is $1/100 =$ **1% of the box**. * **B** and **C** sit in quiet water. Their clouds are wide, and both cover the *same* 20% of the box. Where they overlap the density is $1/0.2 + 1/0.2 = 10$, so each gets $1/10 =$ **10%**. They split the area they share. ::: {#cell-fig-abc .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Flat clouds (rectangles) and the resulting weights. A's thin jet ribbon earns it 1 percent of the box; B and C share one 20 percent cloud, 10 percent each.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-abc-output-1.png){#fig-abc width=450 height=450} ::: ::: ::: {#00c8b1c0 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
float cloud_area density weight
A 0.01 100.0 0.01
B 0.20 10.0 0.10
C 0.20 10.0 0.10
``` ::: ::: If B had been alone, it would have received the full 20%. The weights add to 21%, which is the part of the box the floats can speak for. The remaining 79% is a **gap**, and only a map can fill it. ## Example 2: why this removes the warm bias The south half of the box is warm ($Z=+1$) and the north half cold ($Z=-1$), so the true box mean is $0$. Convergence has collected three floats in the warm half and left one in the cold half. * The three warm floats' clouds each cover the warm half (50%). Stacked density is $3 \times 1/0.5 = 6$, so each gets weight $1/6 \approx 17\%$. **Together they get 50%.** * The lone cold float's cloud covers the cold half. Its density is $1/0.5 = 2$, so it gets **50%** by itself. ::: {#cell-fig-warm .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Three crowded warm floats share the warm half; the lone cold float stands in for the whole cold half.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-warm-output-1.png){#fig-warm width=480 height=450} ::: ::: | | calculation | box mean | |---|---|---| | simple average | $(1+1+1-1)/4$ | \+0\.50 | | reweighted | $3 \times \tfrac16 \times (+1) + \tfrac12 \times (-1)$ | \+0\.00 | | truth | | $0$ | Crowding no longer buys extra influence: three floats in the same place count as one area, not three. ## Example 3: real clouds in the toy jet Real clouds are not rectangles. The currents shape them: * in a jet a cloud is a long thin ribbon: certain to stay in the jet, but unsure how far along it; * among eddies a cloud spreads wide and can split; * in quiet water a cloud stays compact. ::: {#cell-fig-clouds .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Particle clouds from three anchors (stars) after 1, 4 and 16 ten-day cycles, over the heat-content field (red warm, blue cold). Blue: jet core. Orange: eddy flank. Green: quiet water.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-clouds-output-1.png){#fig-clouds width=1419 height=385} ::: ::: Running the full recipe on one snapshot of 60 floats in the toy jet (details in [the full toy report](simex.qmd)) gives the picture below. Floats that drifted into the warm south sit under heavily stacked clouds and get small weights; the few in the cold north get large ones. ::: {#cell-fig-snapshot .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: stacked cloud density (darker = more floats expected) with each float drawn at a size proportional to its weight; outside the black line no cloud reaches. Right: each float's weight relative to an equal share, against its heat content.](simex_intro_files/figure-html/fig-snapshot-output-1.png){#fig-snapshot width=1309 height=429} ::: ::: On this snapshot the simple average is \+0\.47, the reweighted average is \+0\.01, and the truth is \+0\.00. ## When it goes wrong Averaged over 40 repeats of the toy (looking back 4 cycles): ::: {#25ea280c .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
scenario estimator average error (truth = 0)
(any) simple mean 0.42
(any) kriging 0.14
correct model reweighted -0.05
model misses convergence reweighted 0.13
model eddies displaced reweighted 0.03
noise too small (K/4) reweighted -0.10
noise too large (4K) reweighted 0.20
``` ::: ::: * **Model right:** the error is close to zero. The small negative value comes from using only 100 particles per cloud and goes away with more. * **Clouds too narrow** (noise too small): a float landing just outside its own cloud looks like a rare event and gets a huge weight. * **Clouds too wide** (noise too large): every float gets about the same weight, which slides back toward the simple average. * **Model eddies in the wrong place:** a float trapped in a real warm eddy lands where the model says it shouldn't, so it is overweighted. * **Looking back too far** when the model misses some drift: the error creeps back toward the simple average. * **Looking back too little:** the clouds are small, gaps open where floats avoid, and the weights cannot reach the gaps. The [full toy report](simex.qmd) has the details, including a version that combines the weights with a kriged map, which further reduces both the error and the noise.
